ZUNIONSTORE uses AGGREGATE SUM by default, so duplicate payloads have their timestamps added, potentially causing newer spans to be evicted instead of older spans
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key() applies math.floor/math.ceil to datetime fields, causing optimized audit-log requests to fail while building cursors
The advanced paginator path passes negative slice indexes to Django querysets, which reject negative indexing and raise an exception for cursors with negative offsets

adjudication_records.issue_text: Existing Redis buffer keys are sets, but the new code uses ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE; live or rolling deployments with SADD writers will fail with WRONGTYPE until old keys expire

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a clear change in Redis data structure usage. In buffer.py, the code changes from using sets (sadd, scard, sscan, sunionstore) to sorted sets (zadd, zcard, zscan, zunionstore). Similarly, add-buffer.lua changes from scard/sunionstore to zcard/zunionstore. During a rolling deployment, old code instances will still write with SADD (creating set keys), while new code instances will try to use ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE on those same keys. Redis will return WRONGTYPE errors because you cannot use sorted set commands on regular set keys. This is a real deployment compatibility issue that would cause failures until all old keys expire.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ZUNIONSTORE uses AGGREGATE SUM by default, so duplicate payloads have their timestamps added, potentially causing newer spans to be evicted instead of older spans

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ZUNIONSTORE being used in add-buffer.lua (lines like `span_count = redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)`). ZUNIONSTORE by default uses AGGREGATE SUM, meaning if the same payload appears in both sets being merged, their scores (timestamps) will be added together. This corrupts the timestamp ordering. Later, `zpopmin` is used to evict spans when count > 1000, which removes elements with the lowest scores. If duplicate payloads had their timestamps summed, they would have artificially high scores and be retained, while legitimately newer spans with correct (lower) timestamps could be evicted. This is a real correctness bug in the span ordering/eviction logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Reducing redirect traversal from 10,000 to 1,000 leaves deeper parent chains partially resolved and can attach spans to the wrong segment

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the loop limit in add-buffer.lua being reduced from 10,000 to 1,000 iterations (line 30: 'for i = 0, 1000 do'). The original comment explicitly stated 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' By reducing this to 1,000, any span trees with depth between 1,000 and 10,000 will now fail to be properly joined. The loop is used to traverse redirect chains to find the correct set_span_id, and if it terminates early due to the lower limit, spans will be attached to intermediate nodes rather than the correct root segment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Buffer tests do not cover the 1,000-span eviction boundary or verify that the oldest scores are removed

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows new eviction logic in add-buffer.lua (lines checking 'if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)'). This is new functionality that limits spans to 1000 and evicts the oldest ones. Looking at the test files in the diff, none of the test cases add more than 1000 spans or verify the eviction behavior. This is a legitimate missing test coverage concern for newly added nontrivial logic - the 1000-span limit and zpopmin eviction is a significant behavior change that should have test coverage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Buffer tests do not cover duplicate members during ZUNIONSTORE

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a migration from Redis SETs (SADD, SUNIONSTORE, SSCAN, SCARD) to sorted sets (ZADD, ZUNIONSTORE, ZSCAN, ZCARD) in the span buffer code. ZUNIONSTORE with sorted sets handles duplicate members by keeping the one with the highest score (or aggregating based on AGGREGATE option). The tests in the diff add end_timestamp_precise values but don't specifically test the behavior when duplicate span payloads are added with different timestamps, which is a valid edge case for the new sorted set implementation. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for the new functionality, though not a bug in the implementation itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Buffer tests do not cover migration from existing set-typed Redis keys

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a migration from Redis SET operations (sadd, scard, sscan, sunionstore) to SORTED SET operations (zadd, zcard, zscan, zunionstore) in buffer.py and add-buffer.lua. This is a significant data structure change. The finding correctly identifies that the tests don't cover the migration scenario where existing Redis keys might still be SET-typed from before the migration. Looking at the test files, they only test the new sorted set behavior with fresh data (end_timestamp_precise field added), but don't test what happens when the code encounters old SET-typed keys that might exist in production Redis. This is a valid concern for a production migration scenario.
